subtopic_detail: Escalating from enteral measures to intravenous glucose in symptomatic neonatal hypoglycaemia
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar called to the postnatal ward to see a term boy who is four hours old. His mother has type 2 diabetes managed with metformin and insulin through the pregnancy.

He was born in good condition at 4.2 kg. The midwives began hourly glucose monitoring under the unit protocol, offered an early breastfeed and then gave buccal glucose gel after the first low reading, followed by a second feed. He is now jittery with a high pitched cry and will not settle at the breast, and his most recent glucose is lower than the one before. He is pink and well perfused with no respiratory distress.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 158/min, blood pressure 62/38 mmHg, respiratory rate 52/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Jittery with a high pitched cry, poor latch, well perfused, no respiratory distress, no dysmorphic features
data_table.Glucose trend: 1.9 mmol/L at one hour, 1.8 mmol/L after glucose gel and a feed, 1.4 mmol/L now
data_table.Birth details: Term birth, birthweight 4.2 kg, mother with type 2 diabetes on insulin

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Give an intravenous glucose bolus and start a maintenance glucose infusion
options.rationale: He is symptomatic with jitteriness and a high pitched cry, and his glucose has continued to fall despite an adequate trial of feeding and buccal gel, which together mandate intravenous treatment. A bolus corrects the immediate deficit while the infusion prevents the rebound fall that follows a bolus given alone. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal hypoglycaemia)

options.text: Offer another breastfeed and recheck the blood glucose in one hour
options.rationale: Repeating enteral measures that have already failed twice allows a symptomatic infant to remain hypoglycaemic for a further hour, with a real risk of neurological injury. Feeding alone is appropriate for an asymptomatic borderline reading that is trending upwards. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal hypoglycaemia)

options.text: Give oral glucose gel and recheck the blood glucose in thirty minutes
options.rationale: Buccal gel is a reasonable first line adjunct alongside feeding and has already been given without effect, so repeating it is unlikely to change the trajectory. It is not sufficient for a symptomatic infant with a falling level. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal hypoglycaemia)

options.text: Start intramuscular glucagon and continue three hourly feeding
options.rationale: Glucagon mobilises hepatic glycogen and is reserved for situations where intravenous access cannot be obtained or for suspected hyperinsulinism under specialist direction. It is not the routine first choice when a drip can be sited. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal hypoglycaemia)

options.text: Continue routine feeding as this level is normal at four hours of age
options.rationale: A transient nadir in the first hours is common, but 1.4 mmol/L in a symptomatic infant is well below any accepted operational threshold and is falling rather than recovering. Treating it as physiological is the error that leads to preventable injury. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal hypoglycaemia)

explanation.summary: Infants of mothers with diabetes develop hypoglycaemia because sustained intrauterine exposure to maternal glucose drives fetal pancreatic hyperplasia, and the resulting hyperinsulinism persists after the placental glucose supply is cut at birth. Other at risk groups screened by protocol include preterm, growth restricted and large for gestational age infants, and those with perinatal asphyxia or hypothermia. Management escalates in steps: early and frequent feeding, buccal glucose gel as an adjunct, and intravenous glucose when the infant is symptomatic, when the level is very low, or when enteral measures have failed. The reason symptomatic hypoglycaemia is treated so aggressively is that the immature brain relies on glucose almost exclusively and sustained low levels cause occipital predominant injury with lasting visual and cognitive consequences. Hypoglycaemia persisting beyond the first two or three days is not the expected pattern and should prompt investigation for hyperinsulinism or an endocrine or metabolic cause, with a blood sample collected while the infant is hypoglycaemic.
key_points: Maternal diabetes causes fetal hyperinsulinism that persists after birth
Escalate from feeding to buccal gel to intravenous glucose
Symptoms or a falling level despite enteral measures mandate intravenous treatment
Give an infusion after any bolus to prevent a rebound fall
Persistence beyond a few days warrants investigation for hyperinsulinism
explanation.pearls: Collect the diagnostic sample for insulin, cortisol, growth hormone and ketones while the infant is actually hypoglycaemic, because once the glucose is corrected the results become uninterpretable and the opportunity is lost.

subtopic_detail: Choosing between radiological reduction and laparotomy when peritonism accompanies intussusception
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in the emergency department with a 9-month-old girl whose parents describe episodes through the night where she suddenly screamed, pulled her knees up and went pale, then flopped and dozed between them.

Earlier today she passed a nappy containing dark jelly like material. Over the last two hours she has become much less responsive and her parents say her tummy has gone hard. On examination her abdomen is rigid with generalised guarding and she cries when you barely touch it. Bowel sounds are absent. An ultrasound performed thirty minutes ago confirmed an ileocolic intussusception. Intravenous access is in and fluid resuscitation has begun.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 186/min, blood pressure 74/40 mmHg, respiratory rate 48/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 38.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Rigid abdomen with generalised guarding and rebound, absent bowel sounds, prolonged capillary refill, lethargic
data_table.Investigations: Venous lactate 4.8 mmol/L (less than 2.0), white cell count 21.6 x10^9/L (6.0-17.5)
data_table.Imaging: Ultrasound confirms an ileocolic intussusception with free fluid and absent colour Doppler flow in the intussusceptum

lead_in: What is the most appropriate definitive management?

options.text: Air enema reduction in the radiology department after fluid resuscitation
options.rationale: Air enema is the treatment of choice for the great majority of children and would be right had she presented without peritonism, but insufflating a segment of already compromised bowel risks perforation and tension pneumoperitoneum. The clinical findings, not the imaging, remove this option. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

options.text: Fluid resuscitation and laparotomy because peritonism contraindicates enema
options.rationale: Peritonitis, established shock and perforation are absolute contraindications to radiological reduction, and the absent Doppler flow with free fluid indicates ischaemic bowel that will need inspection and possible resection. Operative reduction allows the surgeon to assess viability, which an enema cannot do. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

options.text: Air enema reduction attempted twice before considering any operation
options.rationale: Repeated delayed attempts are a recognised strategy in a stable child whose first reduction is incomplete, but they presuppose viable bowel and a well perfused patient. Persisting here would delay surgery in a shocked child with ischaemic bowel. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

options.text: Observation with serial examination and repeat ultrasound in six hours
options.rationale: Spontaneous reduction occurs occasionally with small bowel intussusception found incidentally, but never justifies observation in a shocked child with peritonism. Six hours of ischaemic bowel would be catastrophic. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

options.text: Nasogastric decompression with antibiotics and enema in the morning
options.rationale: Decompression and antibiotics are appropriate adjuncts but are preparation for surgery rather than a substitute for it, and deferring definitive treatment overnight allows the ischaemia to progress to perforation. The timing is the error. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

explanation.summary: Intussusception classically affects infants between three months and two years and presents with intermittent episodes of severe pain during which the child draws up the legs and becomes pale, with lethargy between episodes that can dominate the picture and lead to a mistaken diagnosis of sepsis or encephalopathy. Ultrasound is the diagnostic test of choice, and air enema reduction succeeds in the large majority of cases, making this one of the few surgical emergencies of infancy usually treated without an operation. The examination that determines the pathway is abdominal rather than radiological: peritonitis, perforation and persistent shock are absolute contraindications to enema because insufflating compromised bowel can perforate it and cause tension pneumoperitoneum. In those children, and in those where reduction fails, laparotomy allows reduction under vision with resection of non viable bowel and identification of a pathological lead point, which becomes more likely in children outside the typical age range.
key_points: Lethargy between painful episodes is a common and misleading feature
Ultrasound is the diagnostic test and air enema the usual treatment
Peritonitis, perforation or persistent shock contraindicate enema reduction
Absent Doppler flow and free fluid suggest ischaemic bowel
A pathological lead point is more likely outside the typical age range
explanation.pearls: Surgical staff should be alerted before any air enema is attempted, because reduction can perforate the bowel and produce a tension pneumoperitoneum needing immediate needle decompression of the abdomen.

subtopic_detail: Parents declining the routine newborn injection on the postnatal ward
stem:
You are the resident on the postnatal ward asked to speak with the parents of a baby girl born four hours ago at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy and normal vaginal birth.

They have declined the routine intramuscular injection offered by the midwife, saying they do not want their daughter to have an injection so soon after birth and that they have read it is unnecessary in a healthy baby. They are articulate, calm and clearly engaged, and they ask you whether there is any other way of doing this. The mother took no anticonvulsant, antituberculous or anticoagulant medication during the pregnancy. The baby is feeding at the breast and her examination is normal.

data_table.Examination: Term infant, normal newborn examination, no bruising, no cephalhaematoma, feeding at the breast
data_table.Maternal medication: No anticonvulsant, antituberculous or anticoagulant medication during pregnancy
data_table.Birth details: Term, uncomplicated pregnancy, normal vaginal birth, no instrumental assistance

lead_in: What is the most appropriate response to their request?

options.text: Explain the bleeding risk and offer the oral schedule instead
options.rationale: The intramuscular dose is preferred because a single injection provides reliable protection, but where parents decline it an oral course is offered as the next best option rather than leaving the infant with nothing. Parents must understand that the oral regimen requires three separate doses completed over the following weeks and is less effective, particularly in exclusively breastfed infants. (Source: NHMRC: Joint statement on vitamin K administration to newborn infants)
source_refs: NHMRC: Joint statement on vitamin K administration to newborn infants

options.text: Accept their decision and document that they declined it
options.rationale: Documenting refusal without offering the alternative leaves a breastfed infant entirely unprotected against late haemorrhagic disease, which most often presents as intracranial haemorrhage between 2 and 12 weeks with substantial mortality and disability. (Source: NHMRC: Joint statement on vitamin K administration to newborn infants)
source_refs: NHMRC: Joint statement on vitamin K administration to newborn infants

options.text: Give the injection anyway once the parents have left the room
options.rationale: Administering a treatment to a child against the expressed refusal of parents who have capacity and are acting within the range of reasonable decisions is unlawful and destroys the therapeutic relationship. (Source: NHMRC: Joint statement on vitamin K administration to newborn infants)
source_refs: NHMRC: Joint statement on vitamin K administration to newborn infants

options.text: Advise that breastfeeding alone will provide adequate protection
options.rationale: Breast milk contains very little vitamin K, which is precisely why exclusively breastfed infants carry the highest risk of late haemorrhagic disease, so this advice is the opposite of correct. (Source: NHMRC: Joint statement on vitamin K administration to newborn infants)
source_refs: NHMRC: Joint statement on vitamin K administration to newborn infants

options.text: Report the refusal to child protection services before discharge
options.rationale: A considered parental decision about a preventive measure, made with capacity and open to discussion, does not meet the threshold for a statutory report, and treating it as one is disproportionate. (Source: NHMRC: Joint statement on vitamin K administration to newborn infants)
source_refs: NHMRC: Joint statement on vitamin K administration to newborn infants

explanation.summary: Vitamin K deficiency bleeding is rare but devastating, and the late form presenting between 2 and 12 weeks typically manifests as intracranial haemorrhage with high rates of death and permanent disability. Newborns are deficient because placental transfer is poor, gut flora are not yet established and breast milk contains very little vitamin K, which makes exclusively breastfed infants the highest risk group. A single intramuscular dose at birth is the recommended approach because it provides reliable protection with one administration. Where parents decline the injection, an oral regimen of three doses is offered rather than nothing, with clear explanation that it is less effective and depends entirely on completion of the later doses.
key_points: Exclusively breastfed infants are at highest risk because breast milk is a poor source
The late form presents at 2 to 12 weeks, often as intracranial haemorrhage
Oral dosing requires three doses and is less reliable than a single intramuscular dose
Maternal anticonvulsants, antituberculous drugs and anticoagulants further increase risk
explanation.pearls: Make sure the later oral doses are actually scheduled and handed over to the community provider before discharge: the failures of the oral regimen in practice are almost entirely failures of completion, not failures of the drug.

sources.label: NHMRC: Joint statement on vitamin K administration to newborn infants
RCH CPG: Neonatal medication and prophylaxis

subtopic_detail: Recurrent cyanotic episodes provoked by crying in a toddler
stem:
An 18-month-old boy is brought to your clinic by his mother after a fourth frightening episode. She describes that each time he has been told off or has hurt himself, he cries hard, then stops breathing out, goes blue around the lips and goes limp for a few seconds before coming round.

On two occasions his arms and legs stiffened and jerked briefly at the end. He is back to his usual self within a minute or two and has never been drowsy or confused afterwards. The episodes have never happened during sleep and have never started without him being upset first. He was born at term, is meeting his milestones, and examination including cardiovascular examination is normal.

data_table.Examination: Alert and interactive, pale conjunctivae, normal tone and reflexes, normal heart sounds with no murmur, femoral pulses present and equal
data_table.History: Four episodes over three months, each provoked by crying, each lasting under one minute with immediate return to baseline
data_table.Family history: Mother had similar episodes as a young child

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange an electroencephalogram and start sodium valproate
options.rationale: The brief stiffening at the end of an episode is a hypoxic convulsion following the drop in cerebral perfusion, not a primary seizure. Events that are always provoked by an emotional trigger and are followed by immediate recovery without drowsiness are not epileptic, and an anticonvulsant is not indicated. (Source: RCH CPG: Breath holding spells)

options.text: Check a full blood count and ferritin and reassure his mother
options.rationale: The history is diagnostic of a breath holding spell, and the only investigation that changes management is a search for iron deficiency, which is more common in affected children and whose correction reduces the frequency of episodes. Explanation and reassurance, including that the episodes are not harmful and not epileptic, is the other half of management. (Source: RCH CPG: Breath holding spells)

options.text: Refer for a 24 hour electrocardiogram and cardiology review
options.rationale: Cardiac investigation is warranted when episodes occur without warning, during sleep or during exercise, or when there is a family history of sudden death, none of which is present. Here every episode followed a clear emotional provocation. (Source: RCH CPG: Breath holding spells)

options.text: Start oral iron now without any further investigation
options.rationale: Iron is the right direction but treating without measuring commits a child to months of therapy and its adverse effects without knowing whether he is deficient, and leaves no baseline against which to judge response. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

options.text: Arrange urgent magnetic resonance imaging of the brain
options.rationale: Neuroimaging is reserved for focal neurological signs, developmental regression or episodes without a provoking trigger. This child has normal development and a normal neurological examination between episodes. (Source: RCH CPG: Breath holding spells)

explanation.summary: Breath holding spells affect up to 5 percent of young children and are diagnosed on the history alone. The defining sequence is a provoking upset, then vigorous crying, then breath held in expiration with colour change and loss of tone, then rapid and complete recovery. A brief tonic or clonic component at the end is a hypoxic convulsion and does not make the event epileptic. Iron deficiency is the one reversible association worth testing for, because correcting it reduces the frequency of spells.
key_points: Always provoked, always brief, always followed by immediate recovery without a postictal state
Episodes during sleep, at rest or on exertion point away from breath holding and towards a cardiac or epileptic cause
A terminal stiffening or jerk is secondary to cerebral hypoxia, not evidence of epilepsy
Spells resolve spontaneously, usually by school age
explanation.pearls: Measure ferritin, not just haemoglobin: children with breath holding spells are often iron deficient with a normal haemoglobin, and treating to a ferritin above 30 micrograms per litre cuts the frequency of episodes.

subtopic_detail: Breast development before eight years with accelerated growth velocity
stem:
A 6-year-old girl is brought to your general practice because her mother has noticed breast development over the past four months. Her mother is worried that she has also grown out of two pairs of shoes since the start of the year.

She has no headaches and no visual symptoms. There is no vaginal bleeding, no body odour and no acne. She has not been exposed to any creams, gels or tablets belonging to adults in the house. Her height has crossed from the 50th to the 91st centile over eighteen months and her weight has tracked steadily along the 75th centile.

data_table.Examination: Tanner stage 3 breast development bilaterally, no pubic or axillary hair, no cafe au lait macules, normal visual fields to confrontation
data_table.Growth: Height 124 cm on the 91st centile, growth velocity 9 cm per year, weight on the 75th centile
data_table.Investigations: Bone age reported as 9 years against a chronological age of 6 years

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure the family and review her growth in twelve months
options.rationale: Isolated premature thelarche in a girl whose growth velocity and bone age are normal can be observed, but accelerated height velocity with a bone age three years ahead marks true activation of the axis and delay costs final adult height. (Source: RCH CPG: Precocious puberty)

options.text: Request a pelvic ultrasound and repeat the scan in six months
options.rationale: Uterine and ovarian dimensions support the diagnosis but do not separate central from peripheral causes, and a repeat scan in six months postpones definitive assessment while the bone age advances further. (Source: RCH CPG: Precocious puberty)

options.text: Refer to paediatric endocrinology for a gonadotrophin stimulation test
options.rationale: Breast development before 8 years with a growth spurt and advanced bone age requires confirmation of central activation, and the stimulation test distinguishes gonadotrophin dependent puberty from peripheral causes. Referral also allows pituitary imaging to be arranged once central puberty is confirmed. (Source: RCH CPG: Precocious puberty)

options.text: Start a gonadotrophin releasing hormone agonist immediately
options.rationale: Suppression may well be the eventual treatment but committing to it before the axis has been shown to be centrally driven risks treating a peripheral cause that would not respond, and the underlying cause must be sought first. (Source: RCH CPG: Precocious puberty)

options.text: Measure early morning testosterone and adrenal androgens
options.rationale: Androgen measurement is directed at virilisation, and this girl has no pubic or axillary hair, no acne and no clitoromegaly. Her findings are oestrogen driven rather than androgen driven. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Precocious puberty in girls is breast development before 8 years, and the features that separate a benign variant from true precocity are growth velocity and bone age. Isolated premature thelarche with normal height velocity and a bone age matching chronological age can be watched. Accelerated growth with a bone age well ahead of chronological age indicates a genuinely activated axis, which shortens final adult height through early epiphyseal fusion. A gonadotrophin stimulation test confirms central activation and directs whether pituitary imaging and suppression are needed.
key_points: Bone age and growth velocity, not breast stage alone, decide whether referral is urgent
Absent pubic and axillary hair point to an oestrogen driven rather than androgen driven process
Central precocious puberty in girls is usually idiopathic, but imaging is still required after confirmation
Exogenous hormone exposure should be excluded by history before investigation
explanation.pearls: A bone age advanced by more than two years over chronological age is the threshold that moves a girl with early breast development from watchful review to same term endocrine referral, because every further year of unopposed oestrogen costs final height.

subtopic_detail: Two small spherical magnets swallowed an hour apart by a four year old
stem:
A 4-year-old boy is brought to your emergency department by his mother, who saw him put two small silver balls from a desk toy into his mouth and swallow them. She is certain they went down about an hour apart this afternoon.

He is playing happily in the cubicle, is not drooling, and has eaten a biscuit without difficulty. His abdomen is soft and non-tender with normal bowel sounds. An abdominal radiograph shows two spherical radiodense objects 5 mm in diameter lying adjacent to one another in the right lower quadrant, with a thin lucent line visible between them on both projections.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 102 beats per minute, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Comfortable and playing, abdomen soft and non-tender, no guarding, bowel sounds present, tolerating oral intake
data_table.Imaging: Two spherical radiodense objects 5 mm in diameter lying adjacent in the right lower quadrant with a thin lucent line between them on both projections
data_table.Timing: Two ingestions approximately one hour apart this afternoon

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Discharge with advice to check his stools each day
options.rationale: Outpatient observation is correct for a single small blunt object, which passes uneventfully in the great majority of children. Two magnets swallowed separately behave entirely differently because they attract across bowel wall. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign body ingestion)

options.text: Give an osmotic laxative to speed transit through the bowel
options.rationale: Accelerating transit does not separate objects that are already magnetically coupled across loops of bowel, and it delays definitive management while the pressure necrosis continues. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign body ingestion)

options.text: Repeat the abdominal radiograph in 24 hours before deciding
options.rationale: A repeat film is reasonable for a single object that has not progressed, but waiting a day with coupled magnets allows necrosis to progress to perforation, and the objects will not separate on their own. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign body ingestion)

options.text: Refer for urgent surgical removal of both objects
options.rationale: Two or more magnets swallowed at different times lie in different loops of bowel and attract across the intervening walls, causing pressure necrosis, fistula, perforation and volvulus within hours, so removal is required even in a child who appears completely well. The thin lucent line between them indicates interposed tissue rather than direct contact. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign body ingestion)

options.text: Admit for observation with four hourly abdominal examination
options.rationale: Serial examination detects peritonism only after perforation has occurred, which is precisely the outcome the intervention is meant to prevent, and children remain well until late. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign body ingestion)

explanation.summary: A single small blunt foreign body beyond the oesophagus in an asymptomatic child can be managed expectantly, and most pass without incident. Multiple magnets are a distinct and far more dangerous scenario, because magnets swallowed at different times come to lie in separate loops of bowel and attract each other across the intervening walls. The resulting pressure necrosis leads to fistula formation, perforation and volvulus, often within hours, while the child continues to look entirely well. A lucent line between adjacent magnets on both radiographic projections indicates interposed bowel wall rather than magnets stuck together in the same lumen.
key_points: One magnet may be observed; two or more require removal
Ingestion at separate times makes separation into different bowel loops more likely
A child with coupled magnets typically looks entirely well until perforation occurs
A lucent gap between the magnets on both projections suggests interposed tissue
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically whether the magnets were swallowed together or at different times, and whether anything else metallic was swallowed: a single magnet plus a separately ingested metal object such as a coin or a button produces exactly the same coupling injury.

sources.label: Queensland Health: Paediatric foreign body ingestion guideline

subtopic_detail: Delayed walking with calf hypertrophy and a grossly raised creatine kinase
stem:
A 4-year-old boy is referred to your paediatric clinic because he cannot keep up with his kindergarten class. He walked at 20 months and his mother says he has always run oddly and comes up the stairs one foot at a time holding the rail.

She has noticed that to get up off the floor he turns onto his front and walks his hands up his own legs. His speech is mildly delayed but he is socially appropriate. Sensation is normal, there are no fasciculations, and his ankle and knee reflexes are present and symmetrical.

data_table.Examination: Bulky firm calves, proximal weakness of hip and shoulder girdle, Gower sign positive, reflexes present, sensation intact
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 12400 U/L (less than 200), alanine aminotransferase 180 U/L (less than 40), aspartate aminotransferase 210 U/L (less than 40), bilirubin and gamma glutamyl transferase within normal limits
data_table.Growth: Height and weight both on the 25th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Request a muscle biopsy before any genetic investigation
options.rationale: Biopsy was the historical standard but genetic testing now identifies a deletion or duplication in about 70 percent of affected boys without an anaesthetic or an open procedure. Biopsy is reserved for cases where genetic testing is uninformative. (Source: RCH CPG: Duchenne muscular dystrophy)

options.text: Arrange nerve conduction studies and electromyography today
options.rationale: Neurophysiology separates neuropathic from myopathic weakness, but preserved reflexes, normal sensation and a creatine kinase in the thousands have already established a myopathy. It would delay the definitive test without changing the differential. (Source: RCH CPG: Duchenne muscular dystrophy)

options.text: Refer for liver biopsy to investigate the raised transaminases
options.rationale: Alanine and aspartate aminotransferase are released from damaged skeletal muscle as well as liver, and a normal gamma glutamyl transferase and bilirubin point away from hepatic disease. Boys with dystrophinopathy are regularly investigated for liver disease before the muscle origin is recognised. (Source: RCH CPG: Duchenne muscular dystrophy)

options.text: Reassure the parents and review his walking in six months
options.rationale: A creatine kinase 60 times the upper limit of normal with objective proximal weakness is never a normal variant, and delay postpones corticosteroid treatment and cardiac surveillance that alter the disease course. (Source: RCH CPG: Duchenne muscular dystrophy)

options.text: Refer for dystrophin gene testing through a neuromuscular clinic
options.rationale: Proximal weakness with calf hypertrophy, a positive Gower sign and a creatine kinase above 10000 U/L in a boy is dystrophinopathy until proven otherwise, and deletion and duplication analysis of the dystrophin gene is the first line confirmatory test. Confirmation through a neuromuscular service also triggers cardiac and respiratory surveillance and genetic counselling for the family. (Source: RCH CPG: Duchenne muscular dystrophy)

explanation.summary: Duchenne muscular dystrophy typically presents between 3 and 5 years with delayed walking, difficulty with stairs, a waddling gait and a positive Gower sign. Calf pseudohypertrophy reflects replacement of muscle by fat and fibrous tissue rather than true muscle bulk. Creatine kinase is characteristically above 10000 U/L and is often accompanied by raised transaminases of muscle origin, which frequently prompts a fruitless hepatic workup. Genetic testing of the dystrophin gene has replaced muscle biopsy as the first line confirmatory investigation.
key_points: Preserved reflexes with normal sensation and a very high creatine kinase indicate myopathy rather than neuropathy
Raised alanine and aspartate aminotransferase with a normal gamma glutamyl transferase are of muscle origin
Deletion and duplication analysis detects about 70 percent of cases; sequencing finds most of the remainder
Confirmation opens access to corticosteroid therapy, cardiac surveillance and carrier testing for the mother
explanation.pearls: Check a creatine kinase in any boy who is not walking by 18 months or who has unexplained transaminitis; the average age at diagnosis is still around 4 to 5 years despite symptoms usually being present well before then.

sources.label: Australian Medicines Handbook Children's Dosing Companion

subtopic_detail: Microcytic anaemia with pica and loss of acquired skills in a toddler
stem:
A 2-year-old boy is brought to your clinic with three months of irritability, poor appetite and constipation. His family moved six months ago into a weatherboard cottage built in the 1920s that is being sanded and repainted around them.

His mother says he chews the window sills and eats flakes of paint from the floor. She is most worried that he used to say about twenty words and now says only five. He was born at term and his development was previously normal. He drinks about 400 mL of cow milk a day and eats meat three times a week. Iron studies taken by another doctor two weeks ago showed a ferritin of 38 micrograms per litre.

data_table.Examination: Pale, mildly irritable but consolable, abdomen soft with no organomegaly, no neurological focal signs, gait normal
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 92 g/L (110-140), mean cell volume 68 fL (75-87), ferritin 38 micrograms per litre (20-100), reticulocytes 1.2 percent, blood film shows basophilic stippling
data_table.Social: Home built in the 1920s currently being sanded and repainted

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Send a venous blood lead level today
options.rationale: Microcytic anaemia with basophilic stippling and a ferritin that is not low excludes iron deficiency as the explanation, and the combination of pica, renovation of a pre 1970 house, constipation and loss of acquired language points to lead. A venous sample is used because capillary samples are readily contaminated by lead on the skin. (Source: NHMRC: Lead exposure and health effects in Australia)
source_refs: NHMRC: Lead exposure and health effects in Australia

options.text: Request haemoglobin electrophoresis
options.rationale: Thalassaemia trait also gives microcytosis with a preserved ferritin, but it does not cause basophilic stippling with developmental regression, and it would not explain the pica or the constipation. Iron studies have already been done and are not low. (Source: RCH CPG: Anaemia)

options.text: Arrange a coeliac serology screen
options.rationale: Coeliac disease is a reasonable cause of microcytic anaemia with poor appetite, but it usually does so by producing iron deficiency, and the ferritin here is preserved. It does not account for basophilic stippling or for loss of language. (Source: RCH CPG: Anaemia)

options.text: Refer for formal audiology testing
options.rationale: Hearing assessment is essential in any child losing language and should follow, but it does not explain the anaemia, the stippled film or the pica, and it would miss an ongoing and reversible exposure. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental delay)

options.text: Start oral iron and recheck in a month
options.rationale: Empirical iron is the usual response to a microcytic anaemia in a toddler, but with a ferritin of 38 micrograms per litre the anaemia is not iron deficient, and a month of treatment leaves the child in the exposed house. Lead also impairs haem synthesis independently of iron status. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

explanation.summary: Lead poisoning in Australian toddlers is now uncommon but persists where pre 1970 lead paint is disturbed by renovation. The clinical signature is insidious: irritability, constipation, poor appetite, pica and, importantly, loss of previously acquired developmental skills. The haematological clue is a microcytic anaemia with basophilic stippling in a child whose ferritin is not low, which uncouples the anaemia from the usual dietary iron deficiency. Diagnosis is by venous blood lead level, and the first management step is always removal from the source of exposure.
key_points: Basophilic stippling with a preserved ferritin separates lead from ordinary iron deficiency
Renovation of housing built before 1970 is the dominant Australian exposure route
Use a venous rather than capillary sample because skin contamination causes false elevation
Developmental regression, not just delay, should always prompt a search for an acquired cause
explanation.pearls: Australian notification and intervention thresholds start at a blood lead of 5 micrograms per decilitre, and chelation is reserved for levels above 45 micrograms per decilitre or for encephalopathy; below that, removing the exposure is the treatment.

sources.label: NHMRC: Lead exposure and health effects in Australia

subtopic_detail: Collapse at ten days of life with absent femoral pulses
stem:
You are the registrar in a regional emergency department when a 10-day-old boy is brought in by ambulance. His mother says he fed poorly overnight, then this morning went grey and floppy and felt cold to touch from the tummy down.

He was born at term by normal vaginal birth with no antenatal concerns and was discharged well on day two. Brachial pulses are easily felt but femoral pulses cannot be palpated on either side. There is no murmur. Pre ductal saturation is 96 percent in the right hand and post ductal saturation is 88 percent in the right foot. Blood glucose is 3.8 mmol/L and there is no rash.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 186 beats per minute, blood pressure 62/38 mmHg in the right arm, respiratory rate 68 breaths per minute, SpO2 96 percent pre ductal and 88 percent post ductal, temperature 36.1 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Mottled and cool peripheries with capillary refill 5 seconds, liver edge 3 cm below the costal margin, brachial pulses present, femoral pulses impalpable bilaterally, no murmur
data_table.Investigations: Venous lactate 7.2 mmol/L (less than 2), pH 7.18, base excess minus 12, blood glucose 3.8 mmol/L, chest radiograph shows cardiomegaly with pulmonary venous congestion
data_table.Birth history: Term vaginal birth, discharged well on day two, newborn examination documented as normal

lead_in: What is the most important immediate treatment?

options.text: Give a 20 mL/kg sodium chloride 0.9 percent bolus
options.rationale: Large volume loading in a neonate whose shock is obstructive rather than hypovolaemic worsens pulmonary oedema, and the enlarged liver and radiographic congestion already indicate a fluid loaded circulation. Small cautious aliquots may be used but volume is not the treatment. (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital heart disease in the newborn)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Congenital heart disease in the newborn

options.text: Start an intravenous prostaglandin E1 infusion
options.rationale: A collapse in the second week with absent femoral pulses and a saturation step down between the right hand and the foot is duct dependent systemic circulation, and prostaglandin E1 reopens the arterial duct to restore flow to the lower body while transfer is arranged. It is started before echocardiography because the diagnosis is clinical and the duct is closing. (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital heart disease in the newborn)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Congenital heart disease in the newborn

options.text: Start intravenous benzylpenicillin and gentamicin
options.rationale: Late onset sepsis presents similarly and antibiotics should be given after cultures, but they do nothing about a closing duct, and the pre ductal to post ductal saturation gradient with impalpable femoral pulses is structural rather than infective. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis)

options.text: Give intravenous furosemide for the pulmonary congestion
options.rationale: Diuresis addresses a consequence of the obstruction rather than its cause, and reducing preload in an infant dependent on ductal flow to perfuse the lower body can precipitate further collapse. (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital heart disease in the newborn)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Congenital heart disease in the newborn

options.text: Arrange urgent echocardiography before any treatment
options.rationale: Echocardiography defines the lesion and should be arranged, but withholding treatment until it is available in a regional centre costs the hours during which the duct completes its closure. The infusion is both treatment and a diagnostic trial. (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital heart disease in the newborn)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Congenital heart disease in the newborn

explanation.summary: Duct dependent systemic circulation, most often critical coarctation or interrupted aortic arch, presents as circulatory collapse in the first two weeks as the arterial duct closes. The physical signature is absent or weak femoral pulses with easily palpable brachial pulses and a pre ductal to post ductal saturation difference, often without any murmur. A normal newborn examination does not exclude it because the duct is still open at discharge. Prostaglandin E1 reopens the duct and is started on clinical grounds, before echocardiography, in any collapsed neonate in whom the diagnosis is possible.
key_points: Absent femoral pulses with present brachial pulses distinguish it from sepsis
A pre ductal and post ductal saturation difference greater than 3 percent supports a duct dependent lesion
Absence of a murmur does not exclude critical left heart obstruction
Apnoea is a recognised adverse effect of prostaglandin infusion, so airway support must be immediately available
explanation.pearls: Give prostaglandin E1 and take blood cultures and antibiotics at the same time: the two diagnoses are clinically indistinguishable at the bedside, and treating only for sepsis in a duct dependent lesion is fatal within hours.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Congenital heart disease in the newborn

subtopic_detail: Persistent fever thirty six hours after a first immunoglobulin infusion in Kawasaki disease
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar looking after a 3-year-old girl admitted four days ago. She had eight days of fever with bilateral non purulent conjunctival injection, cracked red lips, a polymorphous truncal rash and swollen hands, and was treated with intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg and aspirin.

Her fever settled for about twelve hours and has now returned, with three readings above 38.5 degrees Celsius in the last 36 hours since the infusion finished. She remains irritable. Blood cultures taken before the infusion are sterile at 48 hours, urine culture is negative, and a repeat chest radiograph is clear. The echocardiogram performed yesterday showed a left anterior descending coronary artery z score of 2.8.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 158 beats per minute, blood pressure 92/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 38.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Irritable, peeling skin at the fingertips, lips still cracked, no new rash, no meningism
data_table.Investigations: C reactive protein 118 mg/L (less than 5) rising from 96 mg/L, albumin 26 g/L (35-50), platelets 620 x10^9/L, blood and urine cultures sterile at 48 hours
data_table.Treatment given: Intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg completed 36 hours ago, aspirin continuing

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Add broad spectrum antibiotics and repeat the cultures
options.rationale: Sterile cultures at 48 hours with a clear chest radiograph and negative urine make bacterial infection unlikely, and the mucocutaneous features and rising inflammatory markers fit ongoing vasculitis. Reflexively adding antibiotics here delays the treatment that protects the coronary arteries. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

options.text: Increase the aspirin dose and continue current observation
options.rationale: Aspirin modifies platelet aggregation and provides symptomatic relief but has no effect on the vasculitic process driving aneurysm formation, and observation alone through resistant disease is what allows dilatation to progress. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

options.text: Give a second dose of intravenous immunoglobulin
options.rationale: Fever persisting or recurring more than 36 hours after completion of the first infusion defines immunoglobulin resistance, which affects around 10 to 20 percent of children and carries a substantially higher risk of coronary aneurysm. A second infusion of 2 g/kg is the standard first response, and the rising C reactive protein with falling albumin confirms continuing inflammation rather than a resolving illness. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

options.text: Start infliximab in place of further immunoglobulin
options.rationale: Tumour necrosis factor blockade is an accepted option for disease that resists a second infusion, and some centres use it earlier, but it is not the standard first response to a single episode of resistance in Australian practice. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

options.text: Repeat the echocardiogram before changing any treatment
options.rationale: Serial echocardiography is part of surveillance and will be repeated, but a scan result does not alter the decision to re treat resistant disease, and waiting for it wastes time during which inflammation continues. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

explanation.summary: Immunoglobulin resistant Kawasaki disease is defined by fever that persists or recurs more than 36 hours after the first infusion finishes, and it occurs in roughly 10 to 20 percent of children. It matters because resistance is the strongest predictor of coronary artery aneurysm. The decision to re treat rests on the fever pattern together with inflammatory markers that are rising rather than falling, not on the echocardiogram. Standard management in Australia is a second infusion of 2 g/kg, with corticosteroid or infliximab reserved for children who fail that.
key_points: The 36 hour mark after completion of the infusion defines resistance
A rising C reactive protein with a falling albumin supports continuing vasculitis rather than intercurrent infection
A coronary z score above 2.5 already indicates dilatation and raises the stakes of under treatment
Aspirin does not treat the vasculitis and its dose is not the lever here
explanation.pearls: Do not wait for repeat imaging to decide on re treatment: a coronary z score can be normal on day 5 and aneurysmal by day 14, so the fever and the inflammatory trend, not the echocardiogram, drive the second dose.

subtopic_detail: Escalating withdrawal scores on the third day of life after maternal opioid use
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar on the postnatal ward reviewing a baby girl who is 68 hours old. Her mother has been on methadone throughout the pregnancy and has used no other substances, confirmed by consistent urine testing and antenatal engagement.

The baby has been rooming in with her mother, who is breastfeeding, in a quiet dimmed single room with swaddling and skin to skin contact. Despite this her withdrawal scores have risen over three consecutive assessments and she now has a continuous high pitched cry, cannot settle for more than twenty minutes, and has had loose stools with excoriation of her buttocks. Her weight has fallen 9 percent from birth weight. Her blood glucose is 3.2 mmol/L and her temperature is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 176 beats per minute, blood pressure 64/40 mmHg, respiratory rate 68 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Continuous high pitched cry, marked tremor when undisturbed, increased tone, excoriated buttocks, poor sustained feeding
data_table.Investigations: Blood glucose 3.2 mmol/L, electrolytes within normal limits, septic screen not indicated on clinical assessment
data_table.Scores: Three consecutive withdrawal assessments above the treatment threshold despite optimal non-pharmacological care

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue non-pharmacological care and reassess in 24 hours
options.rationale: Supportive care is the foundation of management and has already been optimised, but three consecutive scores above threshold with weight loss and continuous distress define failure of that approach, and further delay risks dehydration and seizures. (Source: NSW Health: Neonatal abstinence syndrome)

options.text: Start phenobarbital and continue the non-pharmacological care
options.rationale: Phenobarbital is used for withdrawal from non opioid substances or as a second agent when morphine alone is insufficient, and it does not treat the opioid receptor withdrawal that is driving this presentation. (Source: NSW Health: Neonatal abstinence syndrome)

options.text: Advise stopping breastfeeding and start a formula feeding plan
options.rationale: Breastfeeding is actively encouraged for women stable on opioid agonist treatment because the small amount of drug in milk reduces withdrawal severity and shortens treatment, so stopping would worsen the problem. (Source: NSW Health: Neonatal abstinence syndrome)

options.text: Start oral morphine and continue the non-pharmacological care
options.rationale: Scores persistently above the treatment threshold despite optimised environmental care, accompanied by excessive weight loss and inability to settle, are the accepted indication to start an opioid, and oral morphine is the first line agent for withdrawal from a maternal opioid. Non-pharmacological measures continue alongside it rather than being replaced by it. (Source: NSW Health: Neonatal abstinence syndrome)

options.text: Give a naloxone dose and observe the response over four hours
options.rationale: Naloxone is contraindicated in an infant exposed to opioids in utero because it precipitates acute severe withdrawal and can cause seizures. (Source: NSW Health: Neonatal abstinence syndrome)

explanation.summary: Neonatal abstinence syndrome from maternal opioid use typically appears between 24 and 72 hours after birth and is assessed with a structured scoring tool applied consistently. Management begins with non-pharmacological care, and rooming in, breastfeeding, swaddling, low stimulus environments and skin to skin contact substantially reduce the proportion of infants who need medication. Pharmacological treatment is indicated when scores remain above threshold despite optimal supportive care, or when there is excessive weight loss, dehydration or seizures. Oral morphine is first line for opioid withdrawal, with phenobarbital reserved as a second agent or for non opioid withdrawal, and naloxone is contraindicated.
key_points: Onset is typically 24 to 72 hours for short-acting opioids and can be later for methadone
Rooming in and breastfeeding reduce both severity and the need for medication
Treat when scores stay above threshold despite optimised supportive care, or with weight loss or seizures
Naloxone is contraindicated because it precipitates severe withdrawal
explanation.pearls: Keep mother and baby together wherever possible: separation to a special care nursery is associated with higher medication rates, longer stays and poorer breastfeeding outcomes, so the rooming in decision is itself part of the treatment.

subtopic_detail: Mucosal bleeding with an isolated very low platelet count in a previously well child
stem:
A 5-year-old boy is brought to your emergency department because he has been bleeding from the gums since brushing his teeth two hours ago and his mother cannot get it to stop. She noticed a rash over his shins three days ago that she thought was from playing outside.

He had a cold about two weeks ago and has otherwise been well. He is playing with a toy in the cubicle and does not look unwell. There is no fever, no bone pain, no night sweats and no weight loss. There is no lymphadenopathy and no hepatosplenomegaly.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 98 beats per minute, blood pressure 100/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Widespread petechiae and purpura, blood oozing from the gingival margins, blood blisters on the buccal mucosa, no lymphadenopathy, no hepatosplenomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 4 x10^9/L (150-400), haemoglobin 118 g/L (110-140), white cell count 7.2 x10^9/L (5.0-15.0) with a normal differential, blood film shows large platelets with no blasts
data_table.History: Viral upper respiratory illness two weeks ago, no bruising before then

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Observe him without treatment and repeat the count tomorrow
options.rationale: Observation is the correct approach for the majority of children whose bleeding is confined to skin, because the condition is self-limiting and the count matters less than the bleeding. Active mucosal bleeding with blood blisters moves this child out of that group. (Source: RCH CPG: Immune thrombocytopenia)

options.text: Transfuse a pooled platelet unit to control the bleeding
options.rationale: Transfused platelets are destroyed by the same circulating antibody within hours, so they are reserved for life threatening haemorrhage such as intracranial bleeding, given alongside immunoglobulin rather than instead of it. (Source: RCH CPG: Immune thrombocytopenia)

options.text: Arrange a bone marrow aspirate before giving any treatment
options.rationale: Marrow examination is indicated when the history or film suggests leukaemia, such as bone pain, organomegaly, lymphadenopathy or abnormalities in other cell lines, none of which is present here. It is not required before treating a typical picture. (Source: RCH CPG: Immune thrombocytopenia)

options.text: Start a three week tapering course of oral prednisolone
options.rationale: Corticosteroid is an alternative first line agent but acts more slowly than immunoglobulin, and a prolonged course should not be started before marrow infiltration has been excluded because it can partially treat and obscure leukaemia. (Source: RCH CPG: Immune thrombocytopenia)

options.text: Give intravenous immunoglobulin to raise the platelet count
options.rationale: Wet purpura, meaning active mucosal bleeding with buccal blood blisters, is the accepted indication for treatment in childhood immune thrombocytopenia, and immunoglobulin raises the count fastest, usually within 24 to 48 hours. The normal haemoglobin, normal white cell count and film without blasts make marrow infiltration unlikely, so treatment can proceed without a marrow examination. (Source: RCH CPG: Immune thrombocytopenia)

explanation.summary: Childhood immune thrombocytopenia typically follows a viral illness by one to three weeks and produces an isolated thrombocytopenia in a well child with a normal examination. The decision to treat is based on bleeding rather than on the platelet count, so a child with dry purpura confined to the skin is observed even with a count below 10 x10^9/L. Wet purpura, meaning active mucosal bleeding or buccal blood blisters, is the threshold for intervention. Intravenous immunoglobulin raises the count most quickly and avoids the diagnostic problem created by starting corticosteroid before leukaemia has been excluded.
key_points: Treat the bleeding, not the number
Abnormalities in other cell lines, organomegaly, lymphadenopathy or bone pain point to leukaemia and require marrow examination
Platelet transfusion is futile except in life threatening haemorrhage because the antibody destroys transfused platelets
Around 80 percent of affected children recover spontaneously within six months
explanation.pearls: Corticosteroid can partially treat acute lymphoblastic leukaemia and obscure the diagnosis, so if you cannot exclude marrow infiltration on the history, examination and film, choose immunoglobulin or do the marrow first.

sources.label: HSANZ and Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: Immune thrombocytopenia

subtopic_detail: Lethargy and grunting in a child treated for presumed gastroenteritis
stem:
You are the registrar reviewing a 5-year-old boy who returns to your emergency department for the third time in four days. He was diagnosed with gastroenteritis at both previous visits after vomiting and abdominal pain, and was discharged on oral rehydration.

His mother says he has now gone quiet, will not walk to the car, and is breathing in a way she describes as grunting. He has had only two loose stools in four days and no fever since the first day. He had a cold two weeks ago. Two 10 mL/kg fluid boluses given in the last hour have made his breathing worse rather than better, and his liver is now palpable 4 cm below the costal margin.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 172 beats per minute, blood pressure 82/48 mmHg, respiratory rate 48 breaths per minute, SpO2 94 percent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Grunting, cool peripheries with capillary refill 4 seconds, gallop rhythm audible, liver 4 cm below the costal margin, chest clear on auscultation, abdomen soft and non-tender
data_table.Investigations: Venous lactate 4.6 mmol/L (less than 2), sodium 134 mmol/L (135-145), creatinine 58 micromol/L (30-60), venous pH 7.28, chest radiograph shows an enlarged cardiac silhouette with pulmonary congestion
data_table.Response to treatment: Respiratory distress increased after two 10 mL/kg fluid boluses

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange an electrocardiogram and urgent echocardiography
options.rationale: Tachycardia out of proportion to the fluid deficit, a gallop rhythm, hepatomegaly, cardiomegaly on the radiograph and worsening after fluid indicate cardiogenic shock, most likely from myocarditis following a viral illness. An electrocardiogram and echocardiogram establish the diagnosis and guide inotropic support before further volume is given. (Source: RCH CPG: Myocarditis)

options.text: Give a further 20 mL/kg fluid bolus for the poor perfusion
options.rationale: Further volume loading a failing ventricle worsens pulmonary oedema and hepatic congestion, and the deterioration after the first two boluses is itself the clue that the shock is cardiogenic rather than hypovolaemic. (Source: RCH CPG: Myocarditis)

options.text: Start intravenous antibiotics and repeat the septic screen now
options.rationale: Sepsis is a reasonable differential and cultures should be taken, but he has been afebrile for three days and the radiographic and examination findings point to a cardiac cause that antibiotics will not address. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis)

options.text: Arrange an abdominal ultrasound for the palpable liver edge
options.rationale: The enlarged liver is venous congestion from right sided failure rather than a primary hepatic problem, so imaging the liver investigates a consequence and delays the cardiac assessment. (Source: RCH CPG: Myocarditis)

options.text: Start intravenous furosemide and admit him to the general ward
options.rationale: Diuresis may eventually be part of treatment but giving it before the cardiac function is known risks precipitating further hypotension in a preload dependent ventricle, and a general ward is the wrong level of care for cardiogenic shock. (Source: RCH CPG: Myocarditis)

explanation.summary: Paediatric myocarditis is notoriously misdiagnosed as gastroenteritis or respiratory infection, because children present with vomiting, abdominal pain, lethargy and tachypnoea rather than with chest pain. The features that should redirect the diagnosis are tachycardia disproportionate to the degree of dehydration or fever, a gallop rhythm, hepatomegaly, and clinical deterioration after fluid resuscitation. Repeated presentations with a diagnosis that does not fit the trajectory is itself a warning. Management is urgent electrocardiography and echocardiography, cautious fluid handling, inotropic support in a setting with paediatric intensive care, and early discussion with a tertiary cardiac service.
key_points: Worsening after a fluid bolus distinguishes cardiogenic from hypovolaemic shock at the bedside
Hepatomegaly and a gallop rhythm are the two most useful examination findings
Vomiting and abdominal pain are common presenting features in children, not chest pain
A preceding viral illness one to two weeks earlier is typical
explanation.pearls: Treat a third presentation with the same diagnosis as a red flag in its own right: children with myocarditis are commonly discharged twice before the diagnosis is made, and the re presentation itself should trigger a full reassessment rather than a repeat of the previous plan.

subtopic_detail: A rapidly enlarging vascular lesion on the upper eyelid of a three month old
stem:
A 3-month-old girl is brought to your clinic by her father. He shows you photographs taken each fortnight since birth of a red lump on her right upper eyelid, which was a faint pink patch at two weeks and is now raised and bright red.

It now extends far enough to push the upper lid down over the upper part of the pupil when she is upright. It is not ulcerated and is not bleeding. She was born at term, is thriving, and there are no other skin lesions and no midline abnormalities. Her father asks whether they should simply wait for it to disappear, as his sister was told to do with a similar lesion on the arm.

data_table.Examination: Bright red compressible plaque 18 mm across the right upper eyelid, partial mechanical ptosis covering the upper pupil, no ulceration, red reflex present and symmetrical
data_table.Growth: Weight and length both tracking on the 50th centile
data_table.Other findings: No other cutaneous lesions, no midline lumbosacral abnormality, cardiovascular examination normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure the father and review the lesion again at 12 months
options.rationale: Watchful waiting is correct for most of these lesions because the great majority involute without treatment, but a lesion obstructing the visual axis or distorting the cornea causes deprivation amblyopia during the critical period of visual development. (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile haemangioma)

options.text: Start oral propranolol after cardiovascular assessment
options.rationale: A periocular lesion interfering with the visual axis is a recognised indication for systemic treatment, and propranolol is first line, producing colour change and softening within days. Baseline heart rate, blood pressure and examination for cardiac disease are checked before starting because bradycardia, hypotension and hypoglycaemia are the important adverse effects. (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile haemangioma)

options.text: Refer for pulsed dye laser treatment of the raised lesion
options.rationale: Laser penetrates only a few millimetres and is useful for residual telangiectasia after involution or for ulceration, but it does not reduce the bulk of a deep proliferating lesion quickly enough to protect vision. (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile haemangioma)

options.text: Apply a potent topical corticosteroid to the lesion each day
options.rationale: Topical corticosteroid has limited effect on a lesion of this size and depth, and periocular application risks raised intraocular pressure and skin atrophy over months of use. (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile haemangioma)

options.text: Arrange surgical excision of the lesion within the next month
options.rationale: Excision during the proliferative phase is vascular and scarring, and is reserved for lesions that fail medical treatment or for reconstruction of residual tissue after involution. (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile haemangioma)

explanation.summary: Infantile haemangiomas are absent or subtle at birth, proliferate rapidly through the first three to six months and then involute slowly over years, which is why most need no treatment. Treatment is indicated when the lesion threatens function, ulcerates or will leave disfigurement, and the periocular site is the classic functional threat because obstruction of the visual axis or astigmatism from corneal distortion causes amblyopia. Oral propranolol is first line and works within the proliferative window, so referral cannot wait for the natural history to declare itself. Baseline cardiovascular assessment precedes the first dose.
key_points: Proliferation happens in the first three to six months, so the window for effective treatment is short
Periocular, airway, nasal tip, lip and perineal sites are the functionally important ones
Five or more cutaneous lesions warrants abdominal ultrasound for hepatic involvement
Bradycardia, hypotension and hypoglycaemia are the adverse effects that shape monitoring and feeding advice
explanation.pearls: Warn parents that propranolol must be given with or just after a feed and withheld during any illness where the infant is not feeding, because the drug blunts the catecholamine response to hypoglycaemia and fasting is the setting in which seizures have occurred.

sources.label: Australian Medicines Handbook Children's Dosing Companion

subtopic_detail: A rib hump on forward bending in a girl who has not yet started menstruating
stem:
A 12-year-old girl is brought to your general practice by her mother, who noticed while her daughter was trying on a dress that one shoulder blade sticks out more than the other and that the hemlines sat unevenly.

The girl has no back pain, no leg weakness, no numbness and no bladder or bowel symptoms. She is otherwise well and plays netball without difficulty. She has developed breast buds within the last year and has not yet had a period. On forward bending there is an obvious asymmetric prominence of the right posterior chest wall. Her neurological examination including reflexes and abdominal reflexes is normal, and there is no midline skin lesion.

data_table.Examination: Right thoracic rib prominence on forward bending, right shoulder higher than left, no midline skin lesion, normal power sensation and reflexes, abdominal reflexes present and symmetrical
data_table.Symptoms: No pain, no neurological symptoms, no bladder or bowel disturbance

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure the family and review her again in twelve months
options.rationale: A premenarchal girl in the middle of her growth spurt is at the point of most rapid curve progression, so a year of observation without measurement can allow a curve to pass the threshold for bracing or surgery. (Source: RCH CPG: Scoliosis)

options.text: Arrange urgent magnetic resonance imaging of the whole spine
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging is reserved for atypical features such as pain, a left thoracic curve, neurological signs, rapid progression or onset before 10 years, none of which is present here. (Source: RCH CPG: Scoliosis)

options.text: Refer to orthopaedics for standing spinal radiographs
options.rationale: A positive forward bend test requires radiographic measurement of the curve angle because management depends entirely on its magnitude and on remaining growth, and a premenarchal girl at Tanner stage 3 has substantial growth left with correspondingly high progression risk. Standing full length films allow the angle to be measured and a monitoring or bracing plan to be set. (Source: RCH CPG: Scoliosis)

options.text: Refer for a course of physiotherapy and postural exercises
options.rationale: Exercise programs may help symptoms and core strength but have not been shown to alter curve progression, and referring without measuring leaves the curve magnitude unknown. (Source: RCH CPG: Scoliosis)

options.text: Advise her to stop netball until the asymmetry has been assessed
options.rationale: Sport neither causes nor worsens the condition, and withdrawing an adolescent from physical activity carries its own costs without any benefit to the spine. (Source: RCH CPG: Scoliosis)

explanation.summary: Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis is usually detected as asymmetry of the trunk rather than as pain, and the forward bend test demonstrating a rib prominence is the standard screening manoeuvre. Because management is determined by the magnitude of the curve and by how much growth remains, a positive screening examination leads to standing radiographic measurement rather than to observation or therapy. Skeletal maturity markers matter as much as the angle itself: a premenarchal girl at Tanner stage 3 is close to peak height velocity and has the highest risk of progression. Bracing is generally considered for curves in the moderate range in a skeletally immature patient, and surgery for larger curves.
key_points: The forward bend test detects rotation; the radiograph quantifies the curve
Remaining growth predicts progression, so menarchal status and Tanner stage are part of the assessment
Pain, neurological signs, a left thoracic curve or onset before 10 years suggest a secondary cause and warrant imaging of the cord
Exercise and physiotherapy do not alter curve progression
explanation.pearls: Ask about menarche at the first visit: a girl who has not yet menstruated has roughly two more years of significant spinal growth ahead, which is what converts a curve that could be watched in an older adolescent into one that needs close interval follow up.
